I work for a coffee cooperative in the south of Minas Gerais, and every week people ask me why our members are changing the way they farm. The answer is simple: the weather has changed. In the last five years, we have had two long droughts and one frost. Because of the dry seasons, our members lost a large part of their yield, and some families almost lost their farms. So we started a program with three steps. First, we plant trees between the coffee plants, because shade-grown coffee needs less water. Second, we help every smallholder to get a certification. As a result, they can sell to buyers who pay a premium. Third, we measure the water that each farm uses. It is not fast and it is not cheap, but in my view, it is the only way to keep these families on their land.

I buy green coffee for a roaster in Hamburg, and my customers have changed a lot. Ten years ago, they asked me only two questions: what is the price, and what is the quality. Today, the first question is often: where does this coffee come from, and how was it produced? The reason is the new European regulation on deforestation. Due to the new rules, I cannot buy a lot if the exporter cannot show me the exact farm. Some people in my company think that this is just more paperwork. Honestly, I am not convinced. I strongly believe that it is good for everyone. When an exporter can trace every bag, I trust the exporter more, and therefore I am happy to sign longer contracts. For me, a smaller carbon footprint and a clear origin are now part of the quality.
